claims.text: Clinic notes and structured EHR medication histories often contain different medication information.
claims.poster_quote: Clinic notes and structured EHR medication histories often contain different medication information.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Clinic notes and structured electronic health record (EHR) medication history often contain different medication information.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in the abstract of the paper.

claims.text: Discrepancies may arise from normalization errors, terminology differences, or documentation timing.
claims.poster_quote: Discrepancies may arise from normalization errors, terminology differences, or documentation timing.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Same-visit disagreement between these sources may result from note-side normalization errors, differences in terminology or timing, or actual differences in documentation.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in the abstract of the paper.

claims.text: This study develops a note-grounded evaluation framework using LLM-assisted reference construction, human review, deterministic normalization, and semantic-temporal comparison with structured records.
claims.poster_quote: This study develops a note-grounded evaluation framework using LLM-assisted reference construction, human review, deterministic normalization, and semantictemporal comparison with structured records.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We developed a note-grounded approach that uses large language model (LLM)-assisted reference construction, targeted and random human review, deterministic medication normalization, and semantic and temporal comparisons with structured medication history.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in the abstract of the paper.

claims.text: The goal is to characterize the nature of mismatches rather than treat them as simple errors.
claims.poster_quote: The goal is to characterize the nature of mismatches rather than treat them as simple errors.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: These results show that note-to-structured-medication mismatch can arise from normalization errors, differences in terminology, and differences in documentation timing.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in the abstract of the paper.

claims.text: The study used a frozen cohort of 11,812 visits from 761 patients.
claims.poster_quote: We used a frozen cohort of 11,812 visits from 761 patients, extracting 31,282 candidate medication mentions from 22,483 clinic notes.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We conducted a clinic-note-only evaluation of treatment-context medication normalization using a frozen cohort run of 11,812 eligible visits from 761 patients and 22,483 manifest notes.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.A of the paper.

claims.text: 31,282 candidate medication mentions were extracted from 22,483 clinic notes.
claims.poster_quote: We used a frozen cohort of 11,812 visits from 761 patients, extracting 31,282 candidate medication mentions from 22,483 clinic notes.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In the frozen run, this process produced 10,543 packet notes and 31,282 packet mentions.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.A of the paper.

claims.text: An LLM (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) generated initial canonical labels under deterministic decoding.
claims.poster_quote: An LLM (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) generated initial canonical labels under deterministic decoding, which were then refined via human audit (targeted and random).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Reference mention rows were constructed from clinic-note context through an LLM-bootstrapped, note-grounded workflow. For each packeted clinic-note context, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct [13], deployed locally through vLLM [14], generated schema-constrained JSON output under deterministic decoding (temperature = 0).
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.A of the paper.

claims.text: Initial canonical labels generated by the LLM were refined via human audit (targeted and random).
claims.poster_quote: An LLM (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) generated initial canonical labels under deterministic decoding, which were then refined via human audit (targeted and random).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A targeted subset of rows was human-audited to improve reference credibility and make the construction process inspectable. In the frozen run, 3,188 of 27,752 reference mention rows were human-audited, corresponding to 11.49% of the reference rows.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.A of the paper.

claims.text: Normalization performance was evaluated on a held-out test set of 5,403 mention rows from 150 patients.
claims.poster_quote: We evaluated normalization performance on a held-out test set of 5,403 mention rows from 150 patients.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To reduce within-cohort adaptation risk for technical performance claims, we introduced a patient-level held-out evaluation track. The 27,752 reference mention rows came from 756 unique patients; these patients were split once into 606 development patients and 150 held-out test patients using a fixed random seed, with approximate balance on patient-level mention-row volume and whether a patient contributed targeted-audit rows.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.B of the paper.

claims.text: The pipeline included surface-exact matching, lexical cleanup, curated alias mapping, and safe decomposition.
claims.poster_quote: The pipeline included surface-exact matching, lexical cleanup, curated alias mapping, and safe decomposition.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The deterministic canonicalization pipeline consisted of surface-exact comparison, lexical cleanup, curated alias mapping, and conservative safe decomposition.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.B of the paper.

claims.text: Note-derived labels were compared with structured EHR using a semantic-temporal ladder: exact, ingredient, broad-category, and ±30/±90-day temporal windows.
claims.poster_quote: We compared note-derived labels with structured EHR using a semantictemporal ladder: exact, ingredient, broad-category, and ±30/±90-day temporal windows.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We used a semantic-temporal ladder to compare each note-derived medication row with structured medication history. Same-visit overlap was checked first in descending semantic specificity: exact canonical label, ingredient or generic overlap, and broad therapeutic-category overlap. If no same-visit overlap existed, the same hierarchy was applied within patient-level ±30-day and ±90-day windows using note date as the primary anchor and visit start date as fallback, followed by any-history overlap.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.C of the paper.

claims.text: OMOP/RxNorm mappings were used for sensitivity analysis.
claims.poster_quote: OMOP/RxNorm mappings were used for sensitivity analysis.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To make the structured-side comparison more reproducible, we also built explicit Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP)/RxNorm-backed mapping artifacts from local OMOP vocabulary tables, including the core concept, relationship, ancestor, drug-strength, and concept-synonym tables.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in Section II.C of the paper.

claims.text: Low same-visit exact agreement does not imply documentation failure.
claims.poster_quote: Low same-visit exact agreement does not imply documentation failure.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Low same-visit exact overlap remained uncommon at 4,563/27,752 = 16.44%. This pattern changes the interpretation of low same-visit exact overlap. Most apparent disagreement was not strict separation between the two documentation sources; instead, it decomposed into same-visit category relatedness and short-window temporal overlap.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: Most mismatches reflect semantic relatedness or temporal displacement, not irreducible discordance.
claims.poster_quote: Most mismatches reflect semantic relatedness or temporal displacement, not irreducible discordance.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Most apparent disagreement was not strict separation between the two documentation sources; instead, it decomposed into same-visit category relatedness and short-window temporal overlap.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: Note-side normalization errors and terminology gaps are major contributors to mismatches.
claims.poster_quote: Note-side normalization errors and terminology gaps are major contributors.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: These results show that note-to-structured-medication mismatch can arise from normalization errors, differences in terminology, and differences in documentation timing.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly stated in the abstract of the paper.

claims.text: The deterministic pipeline’s gain came from institution-specific alias coverage, not generic matching.
claims.poster_quote: The deterministic pipeline’s gain came from institution-specific alias coverage, not generic matching.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On held-out patients, the measurable gain came almost entirely from lexical cleanup and curated alias coverage, while generic lexical retrieval and ontology-only matching recovered less.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.C of the paper.

claims.text: MedXN comparison confirmed that treatment-context evidence requires controlled false positives.
claims.poster_quote: MedXN comparison confirmed that treatment-context evidence requires controlled false positives.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Untuned MedXN produced at least one prediction for 514 of these treatment-context notes. On this MedXN-output subset, the local pipeline achieved precision 0.7317, recall 0.6493, and F1 0.6881, whereas MedXN achieved precision 0.3884, recall 0.7704, and F1 0.5164.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Table III and Section III.C of the paper.

claims.text: Manual review showed 80% of strict no-overlap cases were note-side mapping failures, not undocumented events.
claims.poster_quote: Manual review showed 80% of strict no-overlap cases were noteside mapping failures, not undocumented events.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Manual review of 100 examples from the final OMOP-backed no-overlap bucket further clarified the remaining error surface. Of these reviewed rows, 80 were judged to reflect note-side mapping failure, 7 candidate note-only evidence, 6 structured-side undercapture, and 7 extraction or reference noise.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: The framework distinguishes multiple reasons for mismatch, supporting nuanced clinical interpretation.
claims.poster_quote: The framework distinguishes multiple reasons for mismatch, supporting nuanced clinical interpretation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The strongest supported claim is therefore not that no-overlap proves undocumented medication use, but that the framework distinguishes several reasons why note-derived medication evidence may fail to align exactly with same-visit structured medication history.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section IV of the paper.

claims.text: Limitations include single-center data and LLM-assisted reference construction.
claims.poster_quote: Limitations include single-center data and LLM-assisted reference construction.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Several limitations remain. The cohort comes from a private single-center clinic-note environment, and both the canonical label space and broad medication categories are project-specific. We constructed the reference resource with LLM assistance and targeted and random human review, but did not manually annotate every row.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section IV of the paper.

claims.text: Exact canonical agreement improved from 0.7226 (surface-exact) to 0.8429 after lexical cleanup and alias mapping.
claims.poster_quote: Exact canonical agreement improved from 0.7226 (surface-exact) to 0.8429 after lexical cleanup and alias mapping.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On held-out patients, deterministic alias-aware normalization improved exact canonical agreement from 0.7226 to 0.8429 relative to surface matching.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.C of the paper.

claims.text: Random audit of unaudited rows showed 0.9210 canonical agreement among valid mentions.
claims.poster_quote: Random audit of unaudited rows showed 0.9210 canonical agreement among valid mentions, but treatment-action attribution was lower at 0.5326.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Within this evaluable subset, 536 of 582 rows were canonically correct, yielding canonical agreement of 0.9210 with Wilson 95% confidence interval 0.8962 to 0.9402.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.B of the paper.

claims.text: Treatment-action attribution was lower at 0.5326.
claims.poster_quote: Random audit of unaudited rows showed 0.9210 canonical agreement among valid mentions, but treatment-action attribution was lower at 0.5326.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Action correctness among evaluable valid rows was lower at 310/582 = 0.5326 (Wilson 95% confidence interval 0.4920 to 0.5728), indicating that treatment-action attribution is a harder secondary task than canonical-label assignment.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.B of the paper.

claims.text: Only 16.44% of note-derived rows had same-visit exact overlap with structured records.
claims.poster_quote: Only 16.44% of note-derived rows had same-visit exact overlap with structured records, but 55.17% had same-visit semantic overlap, and 90.34% had overlap within ±30 days.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Same-visit exact overlap remained uncommon at 4,563/27,752 = 16.44%.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: 55.17% of note-derived rows had same-visit semantic overlap with structured records.
claims.poster_quote: Only 16.44% of note-derived rows had same-visit exact overlap with structured records, but 55.17% had same-visit semantic overlap, and 90.34% had overlap within ±30 days.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Cumulatively, 55.17% of note-derived mention rows had same-visit semantic overlap.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: 90.34% of note-derived rows had overlap within ±30 days.
claims.poster_quote: Only 16.44% of note-derived rows had same-visit exact overlap with structured records, but 55.17% had same-visit semantic overlap, and 90.34% had overlap within ±30 days.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Cumulatively, 90.34% had same-visit or ±30-day overlap.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: Under broad mapping, only 3.97% of note-derived rows remained in the strict no-overlap bucket.
claims.poster_quote: Under broad mapping, only 3.97% remained in the strict no-overlap bucket.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Only 1,102/27,752 = 3.97% remained in the strict no-structured-overlap bucket under broad project-level mapping.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: OMOP-backed sensitivity analysis showed strict no-overlap fell from 43.99% to 36.68% after alias supplement.
claims.poster_quote: OMOP-backed sensitivity analysis showed strict no-overlap fell from 43.99% to 36.68% after alias supplement.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On 5,403 held-out test rows, mapped-row coverage increased from 0.6271 to 0.7037, and the strict OMOP-backed no-overlap bucket fell from 2,377 rows (43.99%) to 1,982 rows (36.68%).
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: Residual errors were mostly due to missing aliases (89.32%) and a small set of recurring terms (e.g., acetaminophen, oxycodone).
claims.poster_quote: Residual errors were mostly due to missing aliases (89.32%) and a small set of recurring terms (e.g., acetaminophen, oxycodone).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Among 4,280 unresolved rows after the full deterministic pipeline, missing alias accounted for 3,823 (89.32%), lab/substance or non-medication rows for 345 (8.06%), combination or formulation mismatch for 108 (2.52%), and ambiguous abbreviation for 4 (0.09%). The unresolved raw mentions were also dominated by a small recurring set of medication names: the ten most frequent unresolved terms, led by acetaminophen, oxycodone, ondansetron, dexamethasone, and gabapentin, accounted for 3,751 of 4,280 residual rows (87.64%).
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.F of the paper.

claims.text: Deterministic alias-aware normalization improved exact agreement from 0.7226 to 0.8429 on held-out patients.
claims.poster_quote: On held-out patients, deterministic alias-aware normalization improved exact agreement from 0.7226 to 0.8429.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On held-out patients, deterministic alias-aware normalization improved exact canonical agreement from 0.7226 to 0.8429 relative to surface matching.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.C of the paper.

claims.text: Semantic-temporal analysis revealed that mismatches often reflect terminology, timing, or mapping limits—not missing medication events.
claims.poster_quote: Semantictemporal analysis revealed that mismatches often reflect terminology, timing, or mapping limits—not missing medication events.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Most apparent disagreement was not strict separation between the two documentation sources; instead, it decomposed into same-visit category relatedness and short-window temporal overlap.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section III.D of the paper.

claims.text: This approach enables evidence characterization before clinical inference, improving reliability when comparing clinic notes with structured EHR data.
claims.poster_quote: This approach enables evidence characterization before clinical inference, improving reliability when comparing clinic notes with structured EHR data.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: These results suggest that evidence characterization should precede downstream clinical inference when clinic-note medication evidence is compared with structured medication history.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section IV of the paper.

claims.text: Future work should test portability across institutions and extend to other treatment-context entities.
claims.poster_quote: Future work should test portability across institutions and extend to other treatmentcontext entities.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Future work should evaluate portability across institutions, extend public ontology alignment for heterogeneous note labels, and test whether the same framework transfers to other treatment-context entities beyond medications.
claims.reason: This statement is explicitly supported by Section IV of the paper.
